{"id": "5f6d7292-50b7-4183-a5ce-9b85fefa60cc", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_uuieRpN0LNt2MO2xNU8SMo", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Job timeouts\",\"context\":\"# Job timeouts\\n\\nYou can configure a timeout duration for your jobs so that if a job runs longer than that,\\nAWS Batch terminates the job. For example, you might have a job that you know should only take 15\\nminutes to complete. Sometimes your application gets stuck in a loop and runs forever, so you can\\nset a timeout of 30 minutes to terminate the stuck job.\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nBy default, AWS Batch doesn't have a job timeout. If you don't define a job timeout, the job\\nruns until the container exits.\\n\\nYou specify an `attemptDurationSeconds` parameter, which must be at least 60\\nseconds, either in your job definition, or when you submit the job. When this number of seconds\\nhas passed following the job attempt's `startedAt` timestamp, AWS Batch terminates the\\njob. On the compute resource, your job's container receives a `SIGTERM` signal to give\\nyour application a chance to shut down gracefully. If the container is still running after 30\\nseconds, a `SIGKILL` signal is sent to forcefully shut down the container.\\n\\nTimeout terminations are handled on a best-effort basis. You shouldn't expect your timeout\\ntermination to happen exactly when the job attempt times out (it may take a few seconds longer).\\nIf your application requires precise timeout execution, you should implement this logic within the\\napplication. If you have a large number of jobs timing out concurrently, the timeout terminations\\nbehave as a first in, first out queue, where jobs are terminated in batches.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nThere's no maximum timeout value for an AWS Batch job.\\n\\nIf a job is terminated for exceeding the timeout duration, it isn't retried. If a job attempt\\nfails on its own, then it can retry if retries are enabled, and the timeout countdown is started\\nover for the new attempt.\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nJobs that run on Fargate resources can't expect to run for more than 14 days. If the\\ntimeout duration exceeds 14 days, the Fargate resources may no longer be available and the job\\nwill be terminated.\\n\\nFor array jobs, child jobs have the same timeout configuration as the parent job.\\n\\nFor information about submitting an AWS Batch job with a timeout configuration, see Tutorial: submit a job\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/job_timeouts.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"JobTimeout\",\"context\":\"## Contents\\n\\n**attemptDurationSeconds**\\n: The job timeout time (in seconds) that's measured from the job attempt's\\n `startedAt` timestamp. After this time passes, AWS Batch terminates your jobs if they\\n aren't finished. The minimum value for the timeout is 60 seconds.\\n\\n For array jobs, the timeout applies to the child jobs, not to the parent array job.\\n\\n For multi-node parallel (MNP) jobs, the timeout applies to the whole job, not to the\\n individual nodes.\\n\\n Type: Integer\\n\\n Required: No\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/APIReference/API_JobTimeout.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"interface JobTimeoutProperty \u00b7 AWS CDK\",\"context\":\"## Properties\\n\\n| Name | Type | Description |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| attemptDurationSeconds? | `number` | The job timeout time (in seconds) that's measured from the job attempt's `startedAt` timestamp. |\\n\\n---\\n\\n### attemptDurationSeconds?\\n\\n*Type:*\\n`number`\\n*(optional)*\\n\\nThe job timeout time (in seconds) that's measured from the job attempt's `startedAt` timestamp.\\n\\nAfter this time passes, AWS Batch terminates your jobs if they aren't finished. The minimum value for the timeout is 60 seconds.\\n\\nFor array jobs, the timeout applies to the child jobs, not to the parent array job.\\n\\nFor multi-node parallel (MNP) jobs, the timeout applies to the whole job, not to the individual nodes.\\n\\nSee also: http://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-batch-jobdefinition-jobtimeout.html#cfn-batch-jobdefinition-jobtimeout-attemptdurationseconds\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v2/docs/@aws-cdk_cfn-property-mixins.aws_batch.CfnJobDefinitionPropsMixin.JobTimeoutProperty.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verifying against published AWS documentation"}

{"id": "bafc758d-16fc-4caa-99a0-309c0a3bb461", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_PEZkBbV4CyvNwYD203wWaw", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Embodied AI Blog Series, Part 1: Getting Started with Robot Learning on AWS Batch | AWS Physical AI Blog\",\"context\":\"### Monitor job progress\\n\\nYou can use the console or CLI to track status and stream logs.\\n\\n* + Option A \u2013 AWS Batch console\\n 1. Go to **Jobs**, select the `IsaacGr00tJobQueue` job queue and choose **Search**. You should see the job you submitted in the list and its status.\\n 2. Click into the job you submitted and select the *Logging* tab. You should see the logs in real time.\\n + Option B \u2013 AWS CLIProvide the `JOB_ID` (e.g. from the above `batch submit-job` output) and optionally set `REGION` and `PROFILE` to run the following commands. Check job status:\\n\\n ```\\n REGION=<REGION> PROFILE=<PROFILE> JOB_ID=<JOB_ID>; aws batch describe-jobs --jobs \\\"$JOB_ID\\\" \\\\\\n --query 'jobs[0].{status:status,statusReason:statusReason,createdAt:createdAt,startedAt:startedAt,stoppedAt:stoppedAt}' \\\\\\n --output table --region \\\"$REGION\\\" --profile \\\"$PROFILE\\\"\\n\\n ```\\n\\n Once the job is in RUNNING status, you can stream logs in real time:\\n\\n ```\\n REGION=<REGION> PROFILE=<PROFILE> JOB_ID=<JOB_ID>; aws logs tail /aws/batch/job \\\\\\n --log-stream-names \\\"$(aws batch describe-jobs --jobs \\\"$JOB_ID\\\" --query 'jobs[0].container.logStreamName' --output text --region \\\"$REGION\\\" --profile \\\"$PROFILE\\\")\\\" \\\\\\n --follow --region \\\"$REGION\\\" --profile \\\"$PROFILE\\\"\\n\\n ```\\n\\nNote: While your job is running, you can also monitor training progress and visualize metrics in real-time using the evaluation environment described in section 4 below. This allows you to track training performance and inspect checkpoints as they become available, rather than waiting for the entire fine-tuning process to complete\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/physical-ai/embodied-ai-blog-series-part-1/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Introducing new alerts to help users detect and react to blocked job queues in AWS Batch | AWS HPC Blog\",\"context\":\"### Auto terminating stuck jobs\\n\\nThe second way you can act to address blocked job queues is at the level of the job queue itself.\\n\\nBatch now has a `jobStateTimeLimitActions` parameter for job queues that lets you automatically cancel a stuck job after a defined period of time, `maxTimeSeconds`. If you opt to define this parameter, Batch is designed to start the timeout clock ticking when it detects that a job is blocking the queue. Batch will also update the `statusReason` field at this time. Once the stuck job at the head of the queue is cancelled, a \u201c*Batch Job State Change\u201d* CloudWatch event is emitted with the underlying reason. If Batch detects that another job at the head of the queue is blocking the queue, a *\u201cBatch Job Queue Blocked\u201d* CloudWatch event is emitted, and starts a new `maxTimeSeconds` timer to take the action you defined once the limit is reached.\\n\\nHere\u2019s an example showing how to specify that the job queue will wait for a job that is blocked by compute environments having reached maximum capacity for 4 hours (maxTimeSeconds=14400) before cancelling the job.\\n\\n```\\n\\\"jobStateTimeLimitActions\\\": [\\n {\\n \\\"reason\\\" : \\\"MISCONFIGURATION:COMPUTE_ENVIRONMENT_MAX_RESOURCE\\\",\\n \\\"state\\\": \\\"RUNNABLE\\\",\\n \\\"maxTimeSeconds\\\" : 14400,\\n \\\"action\\\" : \\\"CANCEL\\\"\\n }\\n]\\n\\n```\\n\\nTable 1 lists the scenarios we discussed, the output message in CloudWatch Events, and the `jobStateTimeLimitAction.reason` that you can specify to cancel the stuck job in the job queue. The table also lists the \u201c*Batch Job State Change\u201d* CloudWatch event message if the job was automatically canceled.\\n\\n*Table 1: AWS Batch CloudWatch Events messages for blocked job queue events. The **Scenerio** column describes the context Batch determined that a queue was blocked. **Status Parameter** refers to key fields in event messages that are provided for an event. **Status Parameter Value** lists an example value for the corresponding parameter. Note that the CAPACITY:INSUFFICIENT_INSTANCE_CAPACITY message will provide a specific instance type name, not just the one in the example.*\\n\\n| Scenario | Status Parameter | Status Parameter value |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| **All your job queue\u2019s connected compute environments have received insufficient capacity errors.** | CloudWatch Event `statusReason`\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/hpc/introducing-new-alerts-to-help-users-detect-and-react-to-blocked-job-queues-in-aws-batch/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"describe_jobs\",\"context\":\"Batch / Client / describe_jobs\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/botocore/latest/reference/services/batch/client/describe_jobs.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verifying against published AWS documentation"}
